danish.title: Anden bog (1805) — Kapitel 2
paragraphs: »Han kommer!« råbte signalisten i det øjeblik.

Regimentschefen, rødmende i ansigtet, løb hen til sin hest, greb stigbøjlen med skælvende hænder, kastede kroppen over sadlen, rettede sig op, trak sin sabel og med et lykkeligt og resolut ansigt, idet han åbnede munden skævt, beredte han sig til at råbe. Regimentet dirrede som en fugl, der pusler med sine fjer, og blev ubevægeligt.
»Gi-i-ivagt!« råbte regimentschefen med en sjælsrystende stemme, der udtrykte glæde for ham selv, strenghed for regimentet og velkomst for den øverstbefalende, der nærmede sig.

Ad den brede landevej, kantet af træer på begge sider, kom en høj, lyseblå wiener-kaleche, let knirkende i fjederingen og trukket af seks heste i smart trav. Bag kalechen galopperede følget og en eskorte af kroater. Ved siden af Kutuzov sad en østrigsk general i hvid uniform, der tog sig mærkelig ud blandt de russiske sorte. Kalechen standsede foran regimentet. Kutuzov og den østrigske general talte sagte, og Kutuzov smilede svagt, da han med tunge skridt steg ned fra vognen, ganske som om de to tusind mænd, der åndeløst stirrede på ham, og regimentschefen slet ikke eksisterede.

Kommandoråbet lød, og regimentet dirrede igen, da det med en klirren præsenterede gevær. I den dødsstille stilhed hørtes den øverstbefalendes svage stemme. Regimentet brølede: »Vi ønsker Deres ekse... le... le... lence god helse!« og alt blev atter stille. Først stod Kutuzov roligt, mens regimentet bevægede sig; så gik han og generalen i hvidt, ledsaget af følget, mellem rækkerne.

Af den måde, regimentschefen hilste den øverstbefalende på og slugte ham med øjnene, mens han rettede sig tjenstivrig op, og af den måde, han gik bag generalerne gennem rækkerne, foroverbøjet og næppe i stand til at beherske sine rykvis bevægelser, og af den måde, han sprang frem ved hvert ord eller gestus fra den øverstbefalende, stod det klart, at han udførte sin pligt som underordnet med endnu større iver end sin pligt som chef. Takket være hans strenghed og omhu var regimentet, sammenlignet med andre, der havde nået Braunau samtidigt, i glimrende forfatning. Der var kun 217 syge og efternølere. Alt var i orden — undtagen støvlerne.

Kutuzov gik gennem rækkerne og standsede nu og da for at sige nogle venlige ord til officerer, han kendte fra den tyrkiske krig, og indimellem også til soldaterne. Han kiggede på deres støvler og rystede flere gange bedrøvet på hovedet, mens han henledte den østrigske generals opmærksomhed på dem med et udtryk, der syntes at sige, at han ikke bebrejdede nogen, men ikke kunne lade være med at bemærke, hvor slemt det stod til. Regimentschefen løb frem ved hver sådan lejlighed af frygt for at gå glip af et eneste ord fra den øverstbefalende om regimentet. Bag Kutuzov, i en afstand der tillod, at hvert dæmpet ord kunne høres, fulgte omkring tyve mænd af hans følge. Disse herrer talte indbyrdes og lo undertiden. Nærmest den øverstbefalende gik en smuk adjudant. Det var fyrst Bolkonskij (Andrej). Ved hans side gik hans kammerat Nesvitskij, en høj stabsofficer, overordentligt svær, med et venligt, smilende, smukt ansigt og fugtige øjne. Nesvitskij kunne næppe lade være med at le, fremprovokeret af en mørkhudet husarofficer, der gik ved siden af ham. Denne husar, med et alvorligt ansigt og uden et smil eller en ændring i udtrykket i hans stive øjne, iagttog regimentschefens ryg og efterlignede hans mindste bevægelse. Hver gang regimentschefen rykkede sammen og bøjede sig frem, rykkede og bøjede husaren sig frem på nøjagtig samme måde. Nesvitskij lo og puffede til de andre for at få dem til at se på komikeren.

Kutuzov gik langsomt og dorskt forbi de tusinder af øjne, der næsten trillede ud af deres huler for at iagttage deres chef. Da han nåede tredje kompagni, standsede han pludselig. Hans følge, der ikke havde ventet dette, rykkede uvilkårligt tættere på ham.
»Ah, Timokhin!« sagde han og genkendte den rødnæsede kaptajn, der var blevet irettesat på grund af den blå kappe.

Man skulle have troet, det var umuligt for et menneske at rette sig mere op, end Timokhin havde gjort, da han blev skældt ud af regimentschefen, men nu, da den øverstbefalende henvendte sig til ham, strammede han sig i en sådan grad, at det syntes, han ikke kunne have holdt det ud, hvis den øverstbefalende havde fortsat med at se på ham, og derfor vendte Kutuzov, der tydeligvis forstod hans situation og ikke ønskede ham andet end godt, hurtigt blikket bort, og et næppe mærkbart smil gled over hans arrede og oppustede ansigt.
»Endnu en Ismail-kammerat,« sagde han. »En tapper officer! Er De tilfreds med ham?« spurgte han regimentschefen.
Og denne — uden at ane, at han blev spejlet af husarofficeren som i et spejl — rykkede sammen, trådte frem og svarede: »Meget tilfreds, Deres Eksellence!«
»Vi har alle vores svagheder,« sagde Kutuzov smilende og gik videre fra ham. »Han havde en forkærlighed for Bacchus.«

Regimentschefen var bange for at få en bebrejdelse for dette og svarede ikke. Husaren bemærkede i det øjeblik den rødnæsede kaptajns ansigt og indtrukne mave og efterlignede hans udtryk og positur med en sådan nøjagtighed, at Nesvitskij ikke kunne lade være med at le. Kutuzov drejede sig om. Officeren havde tydeligvis fuldstændig kontrol over sit ansigt og nåede, mens Kutuzov vendte sig, at lave en grimasse og derefter antage det mest alvorlige, ærbødige og uskyldige udtryk.
Tredje kompagni var det sidste, og Kutuzov stod en stund i tanker, tilsyneladende forsøgende at huske noget. Fyrst Andrej trådte frem fra følget og sagde på fransk:
»De bad mig minde Dem om officeren Dolokhov, degraderet til menig i dette regiment.«
»Hvor er Dolokhov?« spurgte Kutuzov.

Dolokhov, der allerede havde skiftet til en grå soldaterkappe, ventede ikke på at blive kaldt. Den velskabte, lyshårede soldats skikkelse med de klare, blå øjne trådte frem fra geleddet, gik hen til den øverstbefalende og præsenterede gevær.
»Har De en klage?« spurgte Kutuzov med en let rynke i panden.
»Det er Dolokhov,« sagde fyrst Andrej.
»Ah!« sagde Kutuzov. »Jeg håber, dette bliver en lektie for Dem. Gør Deres pligt. Kejseren er nådig, og jeg skal ikke glemme Dem, hvis De gør Dem fortjent.«

De klare, blå øjne kiggede på den øverstbefalende lige så dristigt, som de havde set på regimentschefen, og syntes med deres udtryk at rive sløret af konvention bort, der adskiller en øverstbefalende så vidt fra en menig.

»Én ting beder jeg Deres Eksellence om,« sagde Dolokhov med sin faste, klingende, afmålte stemme. »Jeg beder om en lejlighed til at sone min brøde og bevise min hengivenhed for Hans Majestæt kejseren og for Rusland!«

Kutuzov vendte sig bort. Det samme smil i øjnene, som da han vendte sig fra kaptajn Timokhin, gled igen over hans ansigt. Han vendte sig bort med en grimasse, som ville han sige, at alt, hvad Dolokhov havde sagt ham, og alt hvad han kunne sige, længe havde været ham bekendt, at han var træt af det, og at det slet ikke var det, han ønskede. Han vendte sig om og gik hen til sin vogn.
Regimentet opløstes i kompagnier, der marcherede til deres anviste kvarterer nær Braunau, hvor de håbede at modtage støvler og tøj og hvile ud efter de hårde marcher.

»De bærer mig vel ikke nag, Prokhor Ignatytj?« sagde regimentschefen, da han indhentede tredje kompagni på vej til kvarteret og red op ved siden af kaptajn Timokhin, der gik i spidsen. (Regimentschefens ansigt, nu da inspektionen var lykkeligt overstået, strålede af ubændig glæde.) »I kejserens tjeneste ... det kan ikke undgås ... man er sommetider lidt hastig ved en parade ... Jeg er den første til at undskylde, det ved De! ... Han var meget tilfreds!« Og han rakte kaptajnen hånden.

»Tænk ikke på det, hr. general, som om jeg ville vove!« svarede kaptajnen, hvis næse blev rødere, mens han viste et smil, der afslørede, hvor to fortænder manglede, slået ud af en geværkolbe ved Ismail.
»Og sig til hr. Dolokhov, at jeg ikke glemmer ham — han kan være ganske rolig. Og sig mig — det har jeg villet spørge om — hvordan opfører han sig, og i det hele taget ...«
»Hvad tjenesten angår, er han meget punktlig, Deres Eksellence; men hans karakter ...« sagde Timokhin.
»Hvad med hans karakter?« spurgte regimentschefen.
»Den skifter fra dag til dag,« svarede kaptajnen. »Den ene dag er han fornuftig, veldannet og godhjertet, den næste er han et vilddyr .... I Polen slog han næsten en jøde ihjel, om jeg må sige det.«
»Åh ja, ja!« bemærkede regimentschefen. »Men man må alligevel have medlidenhed med en ung mand i ulykke. Han har vigtige forbindelser, så bare ...«
»Det skal nok gå, Deres Eksellence,« sagde Timokhin med et smil, der viste, at han forstod sin chefs ønske.
»Ja, selvfølgelig, selvfølgelig!«
Regimentschefen opsøgte Dolokhov i geleddet og holdt sin hest an og sagde til ham:
»Efter den næste affære ... epauletter.«
Dolokhov kiggede sig om, men sagde intet, og det hånlige smil på hans læber ændrede sig ikke.

»Nå, det er godt nok,« fortsatte regimentschefen. »En kop brændevin til folkene fra mig,« tilføjede han, så soldaterne kunne høre det. »Jeg takker jer alle! Gud være lovet!« Og han red forbi det kompagni og indhentede det næste.
»Ja, han er virkelig en god fyr, man kan tjene under ham,« sagde Timokhin til den underordnede ved sin side.
»Med ét ord: en hjerteknægt ...« sagde den underordnede leende (regimentschefen havde fået tilnavnet Hjerternes Konge).
Det glade humør hos officererne efter inspektionen smittede af på soldaterne. Kompagniet marcherede muntert af sted. Soldaternes stemmer hørtes overalt.
»Sagde de ikke, at Kutuzov er blind på det ene øje?«
»Jo, det er han! Helt blind!«
»Nej, kammerat, han ser skarpere end du. Støvler og benviklere ... han lagde mærke til alt ...«
»Da han kiggede på mine fødder, kammerat ... ja, tænkte jeg ...«
»Og den anden med ham, østrigeren, så ud, som om han var smurt ind i kridt — hvid som mel! De pudser ham vel som et gevær.«
»Sig mig, Fedesjón! ... Sagde han, hvornår slagene begynder? Du stod tæt på ham. Alle sagde, at Bonaparte selv var i Braunau.«

»Bonaparte selv! ... Hør bare på det fjols, hvad han ikke ved! Preusserne er nu i oprør. Østrigerne, ser du, slår dem ned. Når de er slået ned, begynder krigen med Bonaparte. Og han siger, Bonaparte er i Braunau! Du er godt nok en tåbe. Lyt bedre efter!«
»Satans kvartermestre! Se, femte kompagni drejer allerede ind i landsbyen ... de har deres boghvedegrød kogt, inden vi når vores kvarter.«
»Giv mig en tvebak, din djævel!«
»Og gav du mig tobak i går? Nå netop, kammerat! Nå ja, det gør ikke noget, her skal du have.«
»De burde gøre holdt her, ellers må vi gå fire verst mere uden at spise.«
»Det var dejligt, da de tyskere gav os et lift! Man sidder bare stille og bliver kørt.«
»Og her, kammerat, er folk rent ud usle. Derovre virkede de alle som polakker — alle under den russiske krone — men her er de rene tyskere.«
»Sangere frem!« lød kaptajnens kommando.

Og fra de forskellige rækker løb en tyve mand frem. En trommeslager, deres leder, vendte sig om mod sangerne og svingede armen og begyndte en lang, trukken soldatersang, der startede med ordene: »Morgenen gryede, solen stod op,« og sluttede: »Frem da, brødre, frem mod æren, ført af fader Kamenski.« Denne sang var komponeret under det tyrkiske felttog og blev nu sunget i Østrig, den eneste ændring var, at ordene »fader Kamenski« var erstattet med »fader Kutuzov.«

Da han havde slynget de sidste ord ud, som soldater gør, og svunget armene, som om han smed noget mod jorden, så trommeslageren — en mager, flot soldat på fyrre — strengt på sangerne og kneb øjnene sammen. Derefter, da han havde forvisset sig om, at alles øjne var rettet mod ham, løftede han begge arme, som om han forsigtigt løftede en usynlig, men kostbar genstand over hovedet, og holdt den dér et par sekunder, inden han pludselig kastede den ned og begyndte:
»Åh, min løvhytte, åh, min løvhytte ...!«

»Åh, min nye løvhytte ...!« faldt tyve stemmer ind, og kastagnettespilleren, trods vægten af sin udrustning, styrtede frem foran kompagniet, gik baglæns og svingede skuldrene og truede med sine kastagnetter, som om han truede nogen. Soldaterne, der svang armene og instinktivt holdt takten, marcherede med lange skridt. Bag kompagniet hørtes lyden af hjul, knirken af fjedre og trampen af hestesko. Kutuzov og hans følge var på vej tilbage til byen. Den øverstbefalende gav tegn til, at soldaterne skulle fortsætte ugenert, og han og hele hans følge viste glæde ved lyden af sangen og synet af den dansende soldat og de glade, kvikt marcherende mænd. I anden geleds højre flanke, forbi hvilken vognen passerede kompagniet, vakte en blåøjet soldat uvilkårligt opmærksomhed. Det var Dolokhov, der marcherede med særlig ynde og djærvhed i takt til sangen og kiggede på de forbikørende, som om han ynkede alle, der ikke i dette øjeblik marcherede med kompagniet. Husarkornetten fra Kutuzovs følge, der havde efterlignet regimentschefen, faldt tilbage fra vognen og red op ved siden af Dolokhov.

Husarkornet Zjerkov havde engang i Petersborg tilhørt det vilde selskab med Dolokhov som leder. Zjerkov havde mødt Dolokhov i udlandet som menig og havde ikke fundet det passende at anerkende ham. Men nu, da Kutuzov havde talt med den menige gentleman, henvendte han sig til ham med den hjertelighed, man viser en gammel ven.
»Min kære ven, hvordan har du det?« sagde han gennem sangen og lod sin hest holde trit med kompagniet.
»Hvordan jeg har det?« svarede Dolokhov koldt. »Som du ser.«
Den livlige sang gav en særlig krydret klang til den frie og lette tone, Zjerkov talte med, og til den bevidste kulde i Dolokhov's svar.
»Og hvordan går det med officererne?« spurgte Zjerkov.
»Udmærket. De er gode fyre. Og hvordan har du sneget dig ind på staben?«
»Jeg blev tilknyttet; jeg er på tjeneste.«
Begge var tavse.

»Hun slap falken fri fra sit brede højre ærme,« lød sangen og vakte en ufrivillig fornemmelse af mod og munterhed. Deres samtale ville sandsynligvis have været en anden, var det ikke for virkningen af den sang.
»Er det sandt, at østrigerne er slået?« spurgte Dolokhov.
»Fanden ved det! De siger det.«
»Det glæder mig,« svarede Dolokhov kort og klart, som sangen krævede det.
»Hør, kom forbi en aften, så tager vi en omgang farao!« sagde Zjerkov.
»Har du for mange penge?«
»Kom nu.«
»Det kan jeg ikke. Jeg har svoret ikke at drikke og ikke spille, før jeg er genindsat.«
»Nå, det holder bare til den første kamp.«
»Vi får se.«
De var atter tavse.
»Kom, hvis du har brug for noget. Man kan i det mindste gøre nytte på staben ...«
Dolokhov smilede. »Ulejlig dig ikke. Hvis jeg har brug for noget, beder jeg ikke — jeg tager det!«
»Nå, lad gå; jeg mente bare ...«
»Og jeg mente bare ...«
»Farvel.«
»Farvel og god helse ...«
»Det er en lang, lang vej. Til mit fædreland ...«

Zjerkov gav sin hest sporerne; den dansede utålmodigt fra fod til fod, usikker på, hvilken den skulle sætte af med, fandt derefter sit leje, galopperede forbi kompagniet og indhentede vognen, stadig holdende takten til sangen.

english.title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter 2
paragraphs: "He's coming!" shouted the lookout at that moment.

The regimental commander, flushing red, ran to his horse, seized the stirrup with trembling hands, threw himself across the saddle, righted himself, drew his saber, and with a happy, determined expression, his mouth opening crookedly, prepared to shout. The regiment stirred like a bird ruffling its feathers, then went perfectly still.
"Atten-TION!" the regimental commander roared in a voice that shook the soul — a voice expressing joy for himself, severity for the regiment, and welcome for the approaching commander.

Down the broad country road, bordered on both sides by trees, came a tall, light-blue Viennese carriage, creaking faintly on its springs and pulled by six horses at a brisk trot. Behind it galloped the staff officers and a convoy of Croatian soldiers. Kutuzov sat beside an Austrian general in a white uniform that looked out of place among the Russian black ones. The carriage halted before the regiment. Kutuzov and the Austrian spoke in low voices, and Kutuzov gave a slight smile as he stepped heavily down from the carriage — as if those two thousand soldiers holding their breath to watch him, and the regimental commander himself, simply didn't exist.

The command rang out, and again the regiment shivered with a jingling sound as it presented arms. Then in the dead silence the commander in chief's faint voice was heard. The regiment roared: "Long life to Your Excel-len-lency!" Then all was silent again. At first Kutuzov stood still while the regiment marched past; then he and the general in white, accompanied by the staff, walked between the ranks.

From the way the regimental commander saluted the commander in chief and devoured him with his eyes, drawing himself up obsequiously — from the way he walked behind the generals through the ranks, bowing forward and barely able to restrain his jerky movements — from the way he leaped at every word or gesture from the commander in chief — it was clear he performed his duties as a subordinate with even greater enthusiasm than his duties as a commander. Thanks to his strictness and dedication, the regiment was in excellent shape compared to others that had arrived in Braunau at the same time. Only 217 men were sick or missing. Everything was in fine order — except the boots.

Kutuzov walked through the ranks, occasionally stopping to say a few friendly words to officers he had known from the Turkish campaign, and sometimes to the common soldiers as well. Looking at their boots, he shook his head sadly several times, pointing them out to the Austrian general with an expression that seemed to say he wasn't blaming anyone but couldn't help noticing how bad things were. The regimental commander rushed forward each time, afraid of missing a single word the commander in chief might say about the regiment. About twenty staff officers followed behind Kutuzov at a distance that let them hear every quietly spoken word. These men talked among themselves and sometimes laughed. Walking closest to the commander in chief was a handsome adjutant — Prince Bolkonsky. Beside him was his friend Nesvitsky, a tall, extremely stout staff officer with a kind, smiling, handsome face and moist eyes. Nesvitsky could barely contain his laughter, which was being provoked by a swarthy hussar officer walking alongside him. This hussar, his face perfectly serious, without the faintest smile or change in his fixed expression, watched the regimental commander's back and mimicked his every movement. Each time the commander lurched forward, the hussar lurched forward in exactly the same way. Nesvitsky laughed and nudged the others to watch.

Kutuzov walked slowly and heavily past thousands of eyes bulging from their sockets to see their commander. When he reached the third company, he suddenly stopped. His staff, not expecting this, crowded in closer behind him.
"Ah, Timokhin!" he said, recognizing the red-nosed captain who had been called out over the blue greatcoat.

It would have seemed impossible for anyone to stand more rigidly at attention than Timokhin had when the regimental commander reprimanded him, but now that the commander in chief addressed him, the captain drew himself up so stiffly it seemed he couldn't have held it a second longer. Kutuzov clearly understood the man's situation and wished him well, so he quickly turned away, a barely perceptible smile crossing his scarred, puffy face.
"Another Ismail veteran," he remarked. "A brave officer! Are you satisfied with him?" he asked the regimental commander.
The regimental commander — unaware that behind him the hussar was mirroring him like a looking glass — snapped forward and answered: "Very satisfied, Your Excellency!"
"We all have our weaknesses," said Kutuzov with a smile, walking on. "He used to be a bit too fond of Bacchus."

The regimental commander was afraid he was being criticized and said nothing. At that moment, the hussar noticed the red-nosed captain's face and sucked-in stomach and mimicked his expression and posture so perfectly that Nesvitsky couldn't help bursting out laughing. Kutuzov turned around. The hussar evidently had complete control of his face — in the instant Kutuzov was turning, he managed to pull a grimace and then snap back to a perfectly serious, deferential, innocent expression.
The third company was the last, and Kutuzov paused, apparently trying to remember something. Prince Andrew stepped forward from the staff and said in French:
[speaking in French] "You asked me to remind you about the officer Dolokhov, reduced to the ranks in this regiment."
"Where is Dolokhov?" Kutuzov asked.

Dolokhov, who had already changed into a soldier's gray greatcoat, didn't wait to be summoned. The well-built, fair-haired soldier with his clear blue eyes stepped forward from the ranks, walked up to the commander in chief, and presented arms.
"Do you have a complaint?" Kutuzov asked, frowning slightly.
"This is Dolokhov," said Prince Andrew.
"Ah!" said Kutuzov. "I hope this will be a lesson for you. Do your duty. The Emperor is merciful, and I won't forget you if you prove yourself."

Those clear blue eyes looked up at the commander in chief just as boldly as they had stared down the regimental commander — as if their gaze could tear away the veil of protocol that separates a commander in chief from a common soldier.

"One thing I ask of Your Excellency," Dolokhov said in his firm, ringing, deliberate voice. "I ask for the opportunity to redeem my fault and prove my devotion to His Majesty the Emperor and to Russia!"

Kutuzov turned away. The same smile flickered in his eyes — the one he'd shown when turning from Captain Timokhin. He turned with a grimace, as if to say that everything Dolokhov had told him, and anything he could possibly say, had long been known, that it all wearied him, and that this was not at all what he wanted. He walked away and got into the carriage.
The regiment broke into companies and marched to their assigned quarters near Braunau, where they hoped to receive boots and clothing and to rest after their grueling marches.

"You won't hold it against me, Prokhor Ignatych?" said the regimental commander, catching up with the third company on its way to quarters and riding up alongside Captain Timokhin, who was walking at the front. The commander's face was now beaming with irrepressible delight, the inspection safely behind him. "It comes with serving the Emperor... sometimes you're a bit sharp on parade. I'm the first to apologize — you know me! He was very pleased!" He extended his hand to the captain.

"Don't mention it, General — as if I'd dare take offense!" the captain replied, his nose growing redder as he smiled, revealing the gap where two front teeth had been knocked out by a rifle butt at Ismail.
"And please tell Mr. Dolokhov I won't forget him — he can rest easy. Oh, and tell me — I've been meaning to ask — how is he behaving himself? And in general..."
"In terms of service, he's quite meticulous, Your Excellency. But his temperament..." said Timokhin.
"What about his temperament?" the commander asked.
"It changes from day to day," the captain answered. "Some days he's sensible, educated, and perfectly pleasant. Other days he's a wild animal. In Poland, he nearly killed a Jew."
"Well, well," the regimental commander remarked. "Still, one should feel for a young man in his situation. He has important connections, after all... So you'll just..."
"I will, Your Excellency," said Timokhin, his smile showing he understood exactly what the commander was getting at.
"Good, good!"
The regimental commander found Dolokhov in the ranks and, pulling up his horse, said to him:
"After the next engagement — epaulettes."
Dolokhov glanced back but said nothing. The mocking smile on his lips didn't change.

"Well, that's that," the commander continued. "A cup of vodka for every man — from me," he added loud enough for the soldiers to hear. "Thank you all! God be praised!" And he rode past the company to catch up with the next.
"He really is a good man — you can serve under someone like that," Timokhin said to the subaltern beside him.
"In a word — a real King of Hearts," the subaltern replied with a laugh, using the regimental commander's well-known nickname.
The cheerful mood of the officers after the inspection was catching, and the soldiers marched on in high spirits. Voices could be heard on every side.
"They said Kutuzov was blind in one eye?"
"That's right! Completely blind!"
"No way, friend — he sees better than you do. Boots and leg wraps... he spotted everything."
"When he looked down at my feet, friend... well, I thought..."
"And that other one with him, the Austrian — looked like he was covered in chalk, white as flour! Bet they polish him up like a cannon."
"Hey, Fedeshen! Did he say when the fighting starts? You were right near him. Everyone's saying Bonaparte himself is at Braunau."

"Bonaparte himself! Listen to this fool, the things he comes up with! The Prussians are mobilizing now. The Austrians are putting them down, see. Once they're dealt with, then the war with Bonaparte begins. And he says Bonaparte's in Braunau! Shows you're an idiot. You should listen more carefully!"
"Damn these quartermasters! Look — fifth company's already turning into the village. They'll have their porridge cooked before we even reach our billets."
"Give me a biscuit, you devil!"
"And did you give me tobacco yesterday? That's what I thought, friend! Well, fine — here you go."
"They should call a halt here, or we'll end up doing another four miles on an empty stomach."
"Wasn't it great when those Germans gave us rides? You just sit there and get pulled along."
"Out here, friend, the people are dirt poor. Back there they were at least Poles — still under Russian rule — but here they're all proper Germans."
"Singers to the front!" came the captain's order.

About twenty men ran out from the ranks to the front. The lead drummer turned to face the singers and, waving his arm, launched into a long, drawn-out soldiers' song that began with "Morning dawned, the sun was rising" and ended with "Onward, brothers, on to glory, led by Father Kamensky." The song had been written during the Turkish campaign, and the only change now that they were in Austria was that "Father Kamensky" had been swapped for "Father Kutuzov."

Having belted out those final words with a soldier's gusto and flung his arms down as though hurling something to the ground, the drummer — a lean, handsome soldier of about forty — glared sternly at the other singers and narrowed his eyes. Satisfied that all eyes were on him, he raised both arms as if lifting some invisible but precious object above his head, held it there for several seconds, then suddenly threw it down and began:
"Oh, my bower, oh, my bower...!"

"Oh, my bower new...!" echoed twenty voices, and the man with the castanets, despite the weight of his full kit, rushed to the front and walked backward before the company, shaking his shoulders and rattling his castanets as if threatening someone. The soldiers swung their arms in time and marched with long, easy strides. Behind the company came the sound of wheels, creaking springs, and horses' hooves — Kutuzov and his staff were heading back to town. The commander in chief signaled for the men to continue at ease, and everyone in his party showed pleasure at the sound of the singing, the dancing soldier, and the smartly marching men. In the second file from the right flank, where the carriage was passing, one soldier drew attention even without meaning to — a blue-eyed man marching with particular grace and confidence in time to the song, looking at those riding past as if he pitied anyone who wasn't marching with the company at that moment. It was Dolokhov. The hussar cornet from Kutuzov's staff — the same one who had been mimicking the regimental commander — dropped back from the carriage and rode up alongside Dolokhov.

Hussar cornet Zherkov had once belonged to the wild crowd Dolokhov led in Petersburg. He had run into Dolokhov abroad after his demotion and hadn't bothered to acknowledge him. But now that Kutuzov had spoken to the gentleman ranker, Zherkov addressed him with the warmth of an old friend.
"My dear fellow, how are you?" he called out over the singing, keeping his horse in step with the company.
"How am I?" Dolokhov answered coldly. "As you see."
The upbeat song gave a special flavor both to Zherkov's breezy familiarity and to the deliberate chill in Dolokhov's reply.
"And how do you get along with the officers?" Zherkov asked.
"Fine. They're decent men. And how did you manage to worm your way onto the staff?"
"I was assigned — I'm on duty."
Both fell silent.

"She let the hawk fly upward from her wide right sleeve," the song went on, stirring an instinctive feeling of courage and high spirits. Their conversation would probably have gone differently if not for the effect of that song.
"Is it true the Austrians have been beaten?" asked Dolokhov.
"Who the hell knows. That's what they say."
"Good," Dolokhov answered, brief and sharp, as the rhythm of the song demanded.
"Listen, come around some evening — we'll play some faro!" said Zherkov.
"What, you have too much money?"
"Come on."
"I can't. I've sworn off. I won't drink or gamble until I get my commission back."
"Well, that's only until the first battle."
"We'll see."
They fell silent again.
"Drop by if you ever need anything. At least the staff can be useful for something..."
Dolokhov smiled. "Don't bother. If I want something, I won't beg for it — I'll take it."
"Well, I didn't mean —"
"And I only —"
"Goodbye."
"Stay well."
"It's a long, long way — to my native land..."

Zherkov touched his spurs to his horse. It pranced excitedly, unsure which foot to start with, then found its stride and galloped past the company to catch up with the carriage, still keeping time to the song.
